posts.title: A cancellation is not one problem

copy.default:
A cancellation is not one problem.

It can mean:

The client still wants the service but the time stopped working.
They need a different practitioner.
They changed their mind.
They cannot afford it right now.
They found another option.
They simply never got around to rebooking.

Those situations should not automatically get the same follow-up.

The useful question is not just:

Who cancelled?

It is:

What state are they in now, and is there a sensible next step we can make easier?

That small shift turns cancellation reporting into something commercially useful.

posts.title: The retention number I would not trust on its own

copy.default:
If somebody showed me one retention percentage and nothing else, I would not know what to do with it yet.

A single number can hide very different problems.

Are first-time clients failing to return?
Are regulars stretching the gap between visits?
Are cancellations not being recovered?
Are certain services creating weaker return patterns?
Are clients leaving without a next appointment?

The headline metric tells you something changed.

The journey tells you where to look.

That is why I increasingly think retention analysis should begin with customer states and transitions, not one blended percentage.

posts.title: The best follow-up can be a better next step

copy.default:
Sometimes the follow-up message is not the real problem.

The next step is.

If a client has to:

Search for the right service again.
Work out who they saw last time.
Find a suitable appointment from scratch.
Call during opening hours.
Repeat information the business already has.

Then a beautifully written reminder can still lead into unnecessary friction.

Before rewriting the copy, I would ask:

How easy is it for this person to do the thing we are asking them to do?

Good follow-up should reduce effort, not just increase message volume.

posts.title: What building Retention School is forcing me to simplify

copy.default:
Building Retention School is forcing me to answer a useful question:

Can I explain retention without hiding behind marketing language?

Because an appointment-led business owner should not need a lifecycle-marketing dictionary to understand where revenue is leaking.

A client left without rebooking.
An enquiry never became an appointment.
A cancellation created an empty slot.
A regular quietly stopped returning.
Capacity is sitting unused.

Those are operationally recognisable moments.

The system can get sophisticated underneath.

The problem should stay simple enough to see.

That is becoming one of my favourite constraints while building this.

posts.title: Empty capacity deserves a diagnosis before a discount

copy.default:
An empty appointment slot does not automatically mean the price is wrong.

Before reaching for a discount, I would want to know why the capacity is empty.

Was demand never there?
Did somebody cancel?
Did a waitlist exist but nobody activated it?
Are regular clients overdue?
Are enquiries getting stuck before booking?
Is the empty time simply unpopular?

Those causes point to different actions.

Discounting is one possible lever.

It should not be the diagnosis.

If the real issue is a broken return or recovery path, cheaper appointments can hide the leak rather than fix it.

posts.title: A CRM field should earn its place

copy.default:
I have started judging CRM fields by a simple standard:

What decision becomes better because this exists?

If the answer is none, the field might just be administrative decoration.

For a client return system, useful data should help answer things like:

What state is this client in?
When should the business act?
What happened last time?
What should stop the workflow?
Who owns the next step?
Did the client return?

More fields do not automatically create more intelligence.

The goal is not to collect everything.

It is to capture enough truth to make the next action better.

posts.title: The client who is overdue is more useful than the client who is inactive

copy.default:
“Inactive client” is often too blunt to be useful.

A person who normally returns every four weeks and is now at week six is different from somebody who visited once eighteen months ago.

Both might be labelled inactive.

Only one may be behaving unusually for their own pattern.

That is why I like the idea of looking for overdue behaviour, not just old dates.

What was normal for this client or this service?
When did they move outside that range?
Is contact appropriate now?

The better the state definition, the less the business has to rely on blanket win-back campaigns.

posts.title: The question I want every automation to survive

copy.default:
Before automating a follow-up, I want it to survive one question:

Would this still feel sensible if a good member of staff knew the full context?

If the answer is no, speed is not the problem.

The decision logic is.

Automation can make a useful action consistent.

It can also make a bad assumption happen perfectly every time.

So I would rather spend longer defining:

Who should enter.
Who should not.
What event starts it.
What event stops it.
When a person should take over.

Then automate.

Judgement first. Repetition second.

posts.title: Five revenue leaks, five different states

copy.default:
Five common revenue leaks in an appointment-led business can look similar on a spreadsheet because all five end with the same visible result:

No appointment.

But the underlying states are different.

1. No rebook
A client completed their appointment without securing the next one.

2. Lapsed client
A previous client moved beyond their expected return window.

3. Cancellation or no-show loss
Booked capacity disappeared and was not recovered.

4. Unbooked enquiry
Intent existed, but the journey stopped before an appointment.

5. Empty capacity
Useful appointment time remains unsold.

Treating all five as “send more marketing” removes the diagnosis.

A Client Return System starts by identifying the state, then deciding what action, if any, should follow.
